question.difficultyReason: Dense historical stimulus with multiple events. Traps (A) and (D) overreach what the passage says; (C) introduces information about analytical capability that the passage does not establish.
question.stimulus: During the construction of the Quebec Bridge in 1907, the bridge's designer, Theodore Cooper, received word that the suspended span being built out from the bridge's cantilever was deflecting downward by a fraction of an inch (2.54 centimeters). Before he could telegraph to freeze the project, the whole cantilever arm broke off and plunged, along with seven dozen workers, into the St. Lawrence River. It was the worst bridge construction disaster in history. As a direct result of the inquiry that followed, the engineering 'rules of thumb' by which thousands of bridges had been built around the world went down with the Quebec Bridge. Twentieth-century bridge engineers would thereafter depend on far more rigorous applications of mathematical analysis.
question.questionStem: Which one of the following statements can be properly inferred from the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bridges built before about 1907 were built without thorough mathematical analysis and, therefore, were unsafe for the public to use.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cooper's absence from the Quebec Bridge construction site resulted in the breaking off of the cantilever.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nineteenth-century bridge engineers relied on their rules of thumb because analytical methods were inadequate to solve their design problems.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only a more rigorous application of mathematical analysis to the design of the Quebec Bridge could have prevented its collapse.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prior to 1907 the mathematical analysis incorporated in engineering rules of thumb was insufficient to completely assure the safety of bridges under construction.

explanations.correct: The passage explicitly says the rules of thumb that had built thousands of bridges went down with the Quebec Bridge, and engineers thereafter adopted more rigorous analysis. From this you can infer those prior rules were not sufficient to fully assure safety.
explanations.A: Too strong — the passage doesn't say bridges were broadly unsafe for public use.
explanations.B: Cooper's location isn't discussed as causal.
explanations.C: The passage doesn't say analytical methods were inadequate; it says engineers relied on rules of thumb.
explanations.D: Too strong — 'only' a rigorous analysis rules out other possible preventions.

source.notes: Verbatim from LSAC public LR sample page. Correct answer E confirmed.

samples.reason: Voice calibration only — paradox-resolve item. Provides a model of the descriptive, non-argumentative stimulus voice typical of MSS.

question.difficultyReason: Paradox: correlation (optional-headlights users are safer) doesn't imply causation (mandating headlights reduces collisions). Resolution requires spotting the self-selection confound.
question.stimulus: In jurisdictions where use of headlights is optional when visibility is good, drivers who use headlights at all times are less likely to be involved in a collision than are drivers who use headlights only when visibility is poor. Yet Highway Safety Department records show that making use of headlights mandatory at all times does nothing to reduce the overall number of collisions.
question.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In jurisdictions where use of headlights is optional when visibility is good, one driver in four uses headlights for daytime driving in good weather.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A law making use of headlights mandatory at all times is not especially difficult to enforce.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only very careful drivers use headlights when their use is not legally required.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There are some jurisdictions in which it is illegal to use headlights when visibility is good.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The jurisdictions where use of headlights is mandatory at all times are those where daytime visibility is frequently poor.

explanations.correct: If only very careful drivers voluntarily use headlights, then their lower collision rate reflects their carefulness, not the headlights. Mandating headlights doesn't make reckless drivers careful, so overall collisions don't drop. This dissolves the paradox.
explanations.A: Frequency of voluntary use doesn't by itself explain why mandatory use fails to help.
explanations.B: Enforcement difficulty is not the discrepancy.
explanations.D: Edge-case legal quirk; doesn't explain the overall data.
explanations.E: If anything this would make mandatory headlights more useful, worsening the paradox.

source.notes: Verbatim from LSAC public LR sample page. Correct answer C confirmed.
